MUJAHID:v2p756/r1.author: Mujāhid b. Jabr
MUJAHID:v2p756/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
MUJAHID:v2p756/r1.claim: Ibn Abbas says a person of discernment is one with intellect, judgment, ability, and restraint.

MUQATIL:89:1-10/r3.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:89:1-10/r3.speaker: author
MUQATIL:89:1-10/r3.claim: The oath suffices for a rational person to recognize its greatness; God then swears that He watches over all, as in 89:14.

FARRA:v3p259#2/r12.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v3p259#2/r12.speaker: author
FARRA:v3p259#2/r12.claim: Ḥijr means reason or restraint; a person of ḥijr controls himself, as though he had been restrained.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p370#2/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p370#2/r1.speaker: قتادة
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p370#2/r1.claim: Qatada glosses hijr as reason or intellect.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p370#2/r2.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p370#2/r2.speaker: الحسن
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p370#2/r2.claim: Hasan instead glosses it as the core of understanding.

TAB-FULL:v24p358#2/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p358#2/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v24p358#2/r1.claim: The oath by these matters is sufficient for a discerning person who understands the Lord; it is enough without resort to weightier oaths.

TAB-FULL:v24p358#2/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p358#2/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v24p358#2/r2.claim: A person of ḥijr is one with reason and self-restraint; the word also describes a ruler's restraint placed on someone's property.

TAB-FULL:v24p358#2/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p358#2/r3.speaker: ابن عباس، مجاهد، الحسن، قتادة
TAB-FULL:v24p358#2/r3.claim: The reported glosses define ḥijr as reason, discernment, intelligence, or forbearance.

TAB-FULL:v24p360/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p360/r1.speaker: قتادة، ابن زيد
TAB-FULL:v24p360/r1.claim: They gloss the phrase as applying to a person of reason and intelligence; Ibn Zayd equates reason and inner understanding while noting their different Arabic usage.

IBNABIHATIM:v10p3425#2/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3425#2/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3425#2/r1.claim: Ibn Abbas says a person of discernment and reason is meant.

IBNABIHATIM:v10p3425#2/r2.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3425#2/r2.speaker: الحسن
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3425#2/r2.claim: Al-Hasan glosses the person of restraint as one possessing forbearance.

IBNABIHATIM:v10p3425#2/r3.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3425#2/r3.speaker: أبو مالك
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3425#2/r3.claim: Abu Malik says the phrase means a barrier against the Fire.

NAHHAS:v5p219/r10.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p219/r10.speaker: قيل
NAHHAS:v5p219/r10.claim: Another explanation of kufr is concealing God's command that oaths be sworn only by Him.

NAHHAS:v5p219/r3.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p219/r3.speaker: قيل
NAHHAS:v5p219/r3.claim: One gloss takes ḥijr as a restraint or barrier.

NAHHAS:v5p219/r4.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p219/r4.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v5p219/r4.claim: The question asks whether an intelligent person sees an oath in these things, magnifying what is sworn by and confirming the oath's subject.

NAHHAS:v5p219/r5.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p219/r5.speaker: بعض العلماء
NAHHAS:v5p219/r5.claim: Some infer from the question and its reverence that the implied oath is by the Lord of dawn, since believers swear only by God.

NAHHAS:v5p219/r6.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p219/r6.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
NAHHAS:v5p219/r6.claim: He forbade swearing by fathers and said one should swear by God or remain silent.

NAHHAS:v5p219/r7.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p219/r7.speaker: عمر
NAHHAS:v5p219/r7.claim: ʿUmar says he never swore by those objects knowingly or while merely transmitting another's oath.

NAHHAS:v5p219/r8.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p219/r8.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v5p219/r8.claim: The pronoun in ʿUmar's remark refers to the oath, understood by the listener; dhākiran means saying it and āthiran means reporting it.

NAHHAS:v5p219/r9.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p219/r9.speaker: قيل
NAHHAS:v5p219/r9.claim: Swearing by other than God is like the polytheists' practice; another explanation says it assigns God a partner in glorification.

THALABI:v10p195/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p195/r1.speaker: author
THALABI:v10p195/r1.claim: Intellect is also called ʿaql because it restrains a person from shameful conduct, and nihā because it forbids what should not be done; ḥijr means restraint.

THALABI:v10p195/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p195/r2.speaker: author
THALABI:v10p195/r2.claim: A person who has commanding control over something is described as possessing ḥijr, as in a judge placing property under restriction.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p265/r24.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p265/r24.speaker: ابن عباس
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p265/r24.claim: ذو حجر means a person of reason.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p265/r25.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p265/r25.speaker: الحسن
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p265/r25.claim: It may mean a person of forbearance.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p265/r26.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p265/r26.speaker: محمد بن كعب
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p265/r26.claim: It may mean a person of religion.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p265/r27.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p265/r27.speaker: أبو مالك
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p265/r27.claim: It may mean a person of covering or restraint.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p265/r28.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p265/r28.speaker: أبو رجاء
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p265/r28.claim: It may mean a person of knowledge.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p265/r29.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p265/r29.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p265/r29.claim: حجر carries the sense of restraint: stone is hard and resistant, a chamber protects its contents, and a ward's حجر restricts his actions, allowing each gloss to convey restraint.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p265/r30.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p265/r30.speaker: مقاتل
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p265/r30.claim: He takes هل as إن, yielding the sense: surely there is an oath for a person of reason.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p498/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p498/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p498/r1.claim: Hal here is emphatic; Ibn Abbas paraphrases the question as an assertion that these things are indeed an oath for a person of understanding.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p498/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p498/r2.speaker: المفسرون وأهل اللغة
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p498/r2.claim: A person with hijr is a person of reason, intelligence, restraint, and sound judgment.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p498/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p498/r3.speaker: أبو عبيدة عن ذي الرمة
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p498/r3.claim: A line by Dhu al-Rumma uses dhu hijr of a person of high standing and sound sense.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p498/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p498/r4.speaker: الفراء
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p498/r4.claim: Arabs call someone dhu hijr when he controls himself; reason is named hijr because it prevents what is wrong, like a restrictive barrier.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p498/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p498/r5.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p498/r5.claim: A discerning person sees signs of God's craft, power, and oneness in the sworn objects, making them worthy of an oath; the oath's answer is that the Lord lies in wait.

WAHIDI-QT:89:5/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-QT:89:5/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-QT:89:5/r1.claim: For a person of reason, the oath is sufficient and convincing.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:89:1-6/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:89:1-6/r5.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:89:1-6/r5.claim: The oath suffices as a compelling argument for a person of reason.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p417#2/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p417#2/r1.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p417#2/r1.claim: The oath is sufficient for a rational person; حجر means reason because it restrains its owner from the forbidden, like عقل and نهى.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p417#2/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p417#2/r2.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p417#2/r2.claim: The answer to the oath is ‘your Lord is ever watchful’; ‘Have you not seen?’ interrupts between oath and answer.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p417#2/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p417#2/r3.speaker: الفراء
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p417#2/r3.claim: Al-Farra explains ألم تر as ‘Have you not been informed?’; al-Zajjaj says ‘Have you not known?’ and reads it as wonder.

KASHSHAF:89:5/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:89:5/r1.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:89:5/r1.claim: The oath concerns the previously sworn objects; the question asks whether a rational person should regard them as worthy of exaltation by oath.

KASHSHAF:89:5/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:89:5/r2.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:89:5/r2.claim: Alternatively, the question asks whether this is a great oath suitable to confirm the matter being sworn to.

KASHSHAF:89:5/r3.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:89:5/r3.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:89:5/r3.claim: Ḥijr means intellect because it restrains a person from heedless conduct, like ʿaql and nuhyah; ḥaṣāh derives from counting and control.

KASHSHAF:89:5/r4.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:89:5/r4.speaker: الفراء
KASHSHAF:89:5/r4.claim: Al-Farraʾ says a person of ḥijr is one who masters and disciplines himself.

KASHSHAF:89:5/r5.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:89:5/r5.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:89:5/r5.claim: The omitted oath answer is that God will punish them, as the later threat of a scourge of punishment indicates.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p749/r10.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p749/r10.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p749/r10.claim: The oath objects ask whether these things merit an oath before a rational person, or whether an oath of this magnitude confirms the claim; حجر means intellect because it restrains recklessness.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p749/r11.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p749/r11.speaker: الفراء
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p749/r11.claim: Al-Farra says a person with حجر is one who controls and disciplines himself.

TABRISI:89:1-30#4/r13.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:89:1-30#4/r13.speaker: author
TABRISI:89:1-30#4/r13.claim: The oath asks whether these signs suffice for a rational person; their wonders and proofs point to divine unity and wisdom.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p109/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p109/r1.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p109/r1.claim: Ḥijr means intellect because it restrains its possessor from wrongdoing; ʿaql and nahy are likewise named for restraining or forbidding.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p109/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p109/r2.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p109/r2.claim: A person of understanding sees in the oath's objects signs of God's oneness and power, worthy of being sworn by.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p109/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p109/r3.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p109/r3.claim: The oath's answer is 89:14; the intervening account of ʿĀd interrupts between oath and answer.

RAZI:89:5/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:89:5/r1.speaker: author
RAZI:89:5/r1.claim: حجر means intellect, named because it restrains a person from what is improper; عقل, نهية, and حصاة likewise suggest restraint or keeping count.

RAZI:89:5/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:89:5/r2.speaker: الفراء
RAZI:89:5/r2.claim: Al-Farraʾ says a person ذو حجر is self-commanding and controlled; intellect is named حجر because it restrains wrongdoing, from the verb for restricting someone.

RAZI:89:5/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:89:5/r3.speaker: author
RAZI:89:5/r3.claim: The question whether there is an oath is rhetorical confirmation, like asking whether a striking proof is evidence.

RAZI:89:5/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:89:5/r4.speaker: author
RAZI:89:5/r4.claim: A discerning person sees extraordinary signs of divine oneness and lordship in the sworn things; their signs point to their Creator.

RAZI:89:5/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:89:5/r5.speaker: القاضي
RAZI:89:5/r5.claim: Al-Qadi argues that the verse’s emphatic oath is by the Lord of these created things, since emphatic oaths are made by God and people are forbidden to swear by them.

RAZI-FULL:v31p150/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p150/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v31p150/r1.claim: Hajr means intellect because it restrains wrongdoing; related terms for reason and understanding also imply restraint or keeping count.

RAZI-FULL:v31p150/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p150/r2.speaker: الفراء
RAZI-FULL:v31p150/r2.claim: Al-Farra says a person with hajr masters and controls himself; reason is named for preventing vice, with a stone-root also suggesting restraint.

RAZI-FULL:v31p150/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p150/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v31p150/r3.claim: The question whether this is an oath for a person of reason rhetorically intensifies the point: a discerning person sees signs of divine unity and lordship in these objects.

RAZI-FULL:v31p150/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p150/r4.speaker: القاضي
RAZI-FULL:v31p150/r4.claim: Al-Qadi argues the oath must actually be by the Lord of these things, since the verse intensifies the oath and a rational person may not swear by created objects.

QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5#2/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5#2/r2.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5#2/r2.claim: The oath nouns are genitive and its answer is omitted; the threat of punishment in 89:13 supplies it.

QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5#2/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5#2/r3.speaker: ابن الأنباري
QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5#2/r3.claim: He says the omitted oath answer is 'Your Lord is ever watchful' in 89:14.

QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5#2/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5#2/r4.speaker: مقاتل
QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5#2/r4.claim: He reads hal in the sense of inna, meaning there is indeed an oath for a person of reason, with hal serving as the oath's answer.

QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5#2/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5#2/r5.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5#2/r5.claim: Alternatively, hal remains a rhetorical question seeking confirmation; the statement emphasizes both the oath and its subject, with 89:14 or an ellipsis as answer.

QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5#2/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5#2/r6.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5#2/r6.claim: Dhī ḥijr means a person with intellect; the explanations 'intellect,' 'forbearance,' and 'protection' converge on reason.

QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5#2/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5#2/r7.speaker: أبو مالك
QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5#2/r7.claim: He interprets a person of ḥijr as one protected from people; Hasan instead glosses it as forbearance.

QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5#2/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5#2/r8.speaker: الفراء
QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5#2/r8.claim: The root ḥ-j-r means restraint: a rational person restrains himself, and a judge's sequestration prevents someone from managing property.

BAYDAWI-FULL:89:4-6/r3.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:89:4-6/r3.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:89:4-6/r3.claim: قسم may mean an oath or its sworn object; عقل is called حجر because it restrains wrongdoing, like عقل, نهية, and حصاة, which evokes ضبط.

BAYDAWI-FULL:89:4-6/r4.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:89:4-6/r4.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:89:4-6/r4.claim: The suppressed oath answer is that they will be punished, inferred from God’s treatment of ʿĀd, the descendants of ʿĀd ibn ʿAwṣ ibn Iram ibn Shem, the people of Hūd, named for their ancestor.

NASAFI-FULL:v4p336#5/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p336#5/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v4p336#5/r1.claim: Ḥijr means intellect, which restrains a person from improper conduct; the question asks whether the intelligent recognize the oath's greatness or its force in confirming the omitted threat of punishment.

NASAFI-FULL:v4p336#5/r2.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p336#5/r2.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v4p336#5/r2.claim: The omitted object of the oath is that the deniers will be punished, indicated by the later question and account of punishment.

QASHANI:89:5/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:89:5/r1.speaker: author
QASHANI:89:5/r1.claim: The rhetorical question denies that worldly intellects can grasp why these things are honored by oath or understand their order and harmony, since fancy clouds their reason.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p467/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p467/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p467/r1.claim: Ḥijr means intellect; al-Farraʾ says a person of ḥijr restrains and protects himself, as though he were enclosed from harm.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p470#2/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p470#2/r6.speaker: مقاتل
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p470#2/r6.claim: Muqatil treats hal as equivalent to “indeed,” but Abu Hayyan objects that this leaves the oath without a sworn assertion; the question instead asks whether a rational person has enough evidence to take heed.

SAMIN-DURR:89:4/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:89:4/r1.speaker: مقاتل
SAMIN-DURR:89:4/r1.claim: Muqatil treats ‘hal’ as ‘inna’, making the statement that there is indeed an oath for a person of reason; the author rejects this because it cannot be the proposition sworn by the preceding oath.

SAMIN-DURR:89:5/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:89:5/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:89:5/r1.claim: Hajr means intellect; the author says its explanation has already been given.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p394/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p394/r1.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p394/r1.claim: A person of حجر is one endowed with reason, intellect, discernment, and religion; reason is called حجر because it restrains improper speech and conduct.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p394/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p394/r2.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p394/r2.claim: The related uses for the sanctuary boundary, Hajr of Yamamah, and a ruler's restriction share the sense of preventing or barring; the Quran uses the same expression.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p394/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p394/r3.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p394/r3.claim: The oath invokes times of worship and worship itself, including pilgrimage, prayer, and other acts by which obedient, humble believers draw near to God.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p414/r7.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p414/r7.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p414/r7.claim: Ḥijr means intellect that restrains its owner from desire and raises him toward guidance; anyone whose reason prevents sins and prompts noble conduct possesses it.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p414/r8.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p414/r8.speaker: ابن جرير
BIQAI-FULL:v8p414/r8.claim: Ibn Jarir says that a person who masters and controls himself is described as possessing ḥijr.

DURR-FULL:v8p503/r13.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p503/r13.speaker: ابن مسعود
DURR-FULL:v8p503/r13.claim: His recitation ran from the dawn oath through the night oath; he said these oaths affirm that the Lord is ever watchful.

DURR-FULL:v8p503/r14.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p503/r14.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v8p503/r14.claim: The person of understanding is one with intellect and restraint.

DURR-FULL:v8p505/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p505/r1.speaker: عكرمة والضحاك
DURR-FULL:v8p505/r1.claim: They agree that the person addressed has intellect and restraint.

DURR-FULL:v8p505/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p505/r2.speaker: الحسن
DURR-FULL:v8p505/r2.claim: He glossed the word as a person of forbearance.

DURR-FULL:v8p505/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p505/r3.speaker: أبو مالك
DURR-FULL:v8p505/r3.claim: He glossed it as a barrier from the Fire.

DURR-FULL:v8p505/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p505/r4.speaker: السدي
DURR-FULL:v8p505/r4.claim: He glossed it as a person of intellect.

DURR-FULL:v8p505/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p505/r5.speaker: الحارث بن ثعلبة
DURR-FULL:v8p505/r5.claim: His poem uses حجر for sound judgment, asking how he can hope to repent when only a discerning young man is expected to repent.

BURSEVI:v10p326#2/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p326#2/r5.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p326#2/r5.claim: The question about an oath for a possessor of intellect confirms the grandeur of the sworn signs and their worth as emphatic evidence; intellect is illuminated by knowledge of reality.

BURSEVI:v10p326#2/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p326#2/r6.speaker: فتح الرحمن
BURSEVI:v10p326#2/r6.claim: Fath al-Rahman glosses the phrase as asking whether the oath is sufficient and adequate for a person of reason.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p122/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p122/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p122/r1.claim: The question confirms that the sworn objects are magnificent and deserve to be sworn by, thereby emphasizing the matter sworn to; “that” points to those objects and its distance exalts them.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p122/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p122/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p122/r2.claim: A second parsing asks whether people of reason accept such oaths as a way to affirm their claims; both readings emphasize the claim, but Alusi finds the first clearer.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p122/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p122/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p122/r3.claim: Hajr means reason because it restrains its possessor from folly; Arabic also names reason ʿaql, nahya, and hasāt for related ideas of restraining, forbidding, or controlling.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p122/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p122/r4.speaker: الفراء
ALUSI-FULL:v30p122/r4.claim: Al-Farra says dhu hijr describes someone who controls and restrains himself.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p122/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p122/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p122/r5.claim: The unstated matter sworn to is that they will be punished, as the following account indicates.

ELMALILI:89:4-7/r10.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:89:4-7/r10.speaker: Fahr-ı Râzî
ELMALILI:89:4-7/r10.claim: Razi reads the interrogative as emphasis: an intelligent person sees the signs in these oath objects, which point to divine unity and lordship and merit an oath through their Creator.

ELMALILI:89:4-7/r11.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:89:4-7/r11.speaker: Kādî
ELMALILI:89:4-7/r11.claim: Qadi says the question implies an oath by the Lord of these matters, since emphatic oath belongs to God and people are forbidden to swear by created things.

ELMALILI:89:4-7/r12.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:89:4-7/r12.speaker: author
ELMALILI:89:4-7/r12.claim: Hijr derives from restraint: reason is called hijr because it prevents its possessor from evil and impropriety; dhi hijr means one of complete intellect.

ELMALILI:89:4-7/r13.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:89:4-7/r13.speaker: author
ELMALILI:89:4-7/r13.claim: Two views explain the oath’s response: it is ‘your Lord is ever watchful’ with intervening verses parenthetical, or it is omitted and the following account of punishment stands in its place.

ELMALILI:89:4-7/r6.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:89:4-7/r6.speaker: author
ELMALILI:89:4-7/r6.claim: The question asks whether these oaths or their objects offer something worth swearing by for a person whose reason restrains wrongdoing; surely they do, as signs of guidance and blessing.

ELMALILI:89:4-7/r7.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:89:4-7/r7.speaker: author
ELMALILI:89:4-7/r7.claim: A complete intellect traces the changing events to their Lord; hearts amid these changes find tranquility only through remembrance of God.

ELMALILI:89:4-7/r8.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:89:4-7/r8.speaker: مُجَاهِد
ELMALILI:89:4-7/r8.claim: One route to the oath’s meaning is Mujahid’s reported identification of the odd as God, making God the greatest object sworn by among these signs.

ELMALILI:89:4-7/r9.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:89:4-7/r9.speaker: author
ELMALILI:89:4-7/r9.claim: Alternatively, each oath object is a divine sign, and the real oath is by the one Lord they indicate, effectively ‘by the Lord of dawn’; the question both denies and affirms to elicit this answer.

QUTB-ZILAL:89:5/r1.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:89:5/r1.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:89:5/r1.claim: The question is rhetorical and confirms that the oath convinces anyone possessing intellect and discernment; the interrogative form also preserves the passage’s hushed delicacy.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p316/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p316/r1.speaker: نافع وأبو عمرو وأبو جعفر
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p316/r1.claim: Their readings do not conflict with the written codex, since its spelling can reflect pausal forms and pauses often affect orthography.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p316/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p316/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p316/r2.claim: The question is parenthetical between the oath and its answer or proof, as in the Quran's oath in al-Waqi'a.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p316/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p316/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p316/r3.claim: Hal is confirmatory here, reflecting its original force of establishing a fact like qad; the demonstrative refers to the objects sworn by.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p316/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p316/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p316/r4.claim: The indefinite qasam magnifies the oath as sufficient and compelling for a rational listener; hijr means intellect because it restrains its possessor from wrongdoing.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p316/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p316/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p316/r5.claim: The lām in ‘for one of reason’ gives the oath its purpose: a rational person should not stubbornly deny the oath-taker's truth.

TABATABAI:89:5-8/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:89:5-8/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:89:5-8/r3.claim: The question points back to the preceding oaths and seeks assent: they suffice for a rational person to distinguish truth from falsehood.

TABATABAI:89:5-8/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:89:5-8/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:89:5-8/r4.claim: Since God swears only by something honored, His oath confirms a truth whose veracity is beyond doubt.

ASAD-NOTES:89:1#n4/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:89:1#n4/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:89:1#n4/r1.claim: The oath is solemn evidence for God's existence and oneness.

BINTSHATI:v2p136/r5.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p136/r5.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v2p136/r5.claim: The author rejects an answer supplied by al-Ghashiya: it was revealed 58 surahs after al-Fajr, so adjacency in the printed order cannot leave this oath suspended until then.

BINTSHATI:v2p136/r6.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p136/r6.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v2p136/r6.claim: The author says the oath is complete in its attention-directing question, so no omitted answer is needed; hijr means reason.

CORPUSCORANICUM:89:1-5:kommentar/r3.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:89:1-5:kommentar/r3.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:89:1-5:kommentar/r3.claim: Unlike 91 and 92, the oath is followed by no explicit contrast of good and evil; its enigmatic question invites the hearer to decode it.

CORPUSCORANICUM:89:1-5:kommentar/r4.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:89:1-5:kommentar/r4.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:89:1-5:kommentar/r4.claim: The moral-eschatological point of the duality is likely resolved by the final announcement of punishment.

CORPUSCORANICUM:89:5:anmerkung/r1.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:89:5:anmerkung/r1.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:89:5:anmerkung/r1.claim: The verse asks literally whether this contains an oath for a discerning person, a metatextual description also found in 56:75–76.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p296/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p296/r1.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p296/r1.claim: The preceding surah's signs establish God's power, wisdom, and providence, which entail a Day of accountability and reward; otherwise His mercy and wisdom would be contradicted.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p296/r2.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p296/r2.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p296/r2.claim: The Prophet's role is to warn through the signs in heaven and earth, even when people cannot see them; he cannot guide the blind.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p299/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p299/r1.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p299/r1.claim: The oaths establish that God alone governs the world, brings things forth and removes them, grants respite, and acts within no rival's authority.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p300/r3.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p300/r3.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p300/r3.claim: Oaths should be read as evidence for the surah's claim, not assumed to concern sacred objects; identify the claim and compare parallel Qur'anic passages.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p301/r2.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p301/r2.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p301/r2.claim: Those demanding immediate proof of Judgment are told that God's signs follow a fixed gradual program and Judgment will arrive at its appointed time.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p304/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p304/r1.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p304/r1.claim: Contrasting forces of nature coexist in harmony; only one wise, powerful sovereign can reconcile them, since competing deities would destroy the world.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p304/r2.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p304/r2.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p304/r2.claim: Pairs reach completion with their counterparts; likewise this world is incomplete without an afterlife, where God will judge the conflict of good and evil and reward or punish people.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p306/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p306/r1.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p306/r1.claim: Ḥijr means intellect; both words carry the sense of restraining or tying up, and intellect is an inner leash against undignified conduct.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p306/r2.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p306/r2.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p306/r2.claim: The interrogative rebukes while decisively asserting that a sensible person should learn from nearby signs instead of waiting to see the Hereafter before believing.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p306/r3.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p306/r3.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p306/r3.claim: After earlier signs failed to convince the stubborn, the most manifest and nearby signs are presented as testimony for the sensible, though the stubborn will not benefit.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:89:1/r11.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:89:1/r11.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:89:1/r11.claim: The root meaning of hijr is “to prevent”; reason shares this name because it restrains false ideas and bad conduct, so understanding divine messages and the oath's purpose requires using reason well.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:89:1/r9.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:89:1/r9.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:89:1/r9.claim: Although the sentence begins with a question particle, commentators agree that it functions like qad, a particle of certainty, underscoring the importance of the oath's objects.

STUDYQURAN:89:5/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:89:5/r1.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:89:5/r1.claim: Dhī ḥijr derives from ḥajara, “prevent” or “prohibit”; ḥijr can mean intellect because it prevents error and confusion.

STUDYQURAN:89:5/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:89:5/r2.speaker: some
STUDYQURAN:89:5/r2.claim: Ḥijr can also mean self-control, or ḥilm.
